marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q001.takeaway: Two synovial joint pairs are associated with the external skull: temporomandibular and lateral atlanto-occipital articulations.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q001.displayText: There are 2 pairs of synovial articulations that are associated with the exterior of the skull. They are the temporomandibular joint and the lateral joints (part of the atlantooccipital joints). Joints of the cranial vault include fibrous joints (sutures), which facilitate growth of the skull and account for the majority of skull joints; primary cartilaginous joints, present between two bones in the skull base; and synovial joints, including the temporomandibular joints and atlantooccipital joints.

rationales.a: One pair would omit the paired lateral atlanto-occipital joints in addition to temporomandibular joints.
rationales.c: Three pairs overcounts; only TMJ and lateral atlanto-occipital articulations are listed as external skull synovial articulations.
rationales.d: Four pairs includes skull sutures or intracranial articulations, which are not synovial exterior joints.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q002.takeaway: The interparietal bone is the Inca bone, often a sutural variant near lambdoid suture.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q002.displayText: The interparietal bone of the skull is known as the Inca bone. It is a sutural bone that lies between the occipital and the parietal bones. Sutural or Wormian bones are islands of bone commonly found within the lambdoid suture in some individuals. They may arise from separate centres of ossification and usually have no clinical significance.

rationales.a: Parietal bone is a main cranial-vault bone but is not the named accessory Inca bone.
rationales.b: Temporal bone forms lateral skull and zygomatic arch, not interparietal region.
rationales.d: Occipital bone adjoins the interparietal bone but the latter itself is the Inca bone.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q003.takeaway: Coronal suture fusion between frontal and parietal bones produces anterior plagiocephaly.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q003.displayText: In anterior plagiocephaly, premature fusion of the coronal suture is seen. The coronal suture is present between the frontal and parietal bones. Major sutures of the skull are: lambdoid suture - between parietal and occipital bones; sagittal suture - between the two parietal bones; metopic suture - between the two frontal bones. Craniosynostosis is congenital premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, resulting in an abnormal head shape.

rationales.a: Metopic suture fuses between the two frontal bones, not in anterior plagiocephaly.
rationales.c: Lambdoid suture lies between occipital and parietal bones and is associated with posterior skull shape.
rationales.d: Sagittal suture separates the two parietal bones; coronal suture is frontal-parietal.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q004.takeaway: Foramen spinosum transmits middle meningeal vessels and nervus spinosus.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q004.displayText: The foramen marked is the foramen spinosum. The structures passing through it are the middle meningeal artery, nervus spinosus and middle meningeal vein.

rationales.a: Accessory meningeal artery usually passes through foramen ovale, not foramen spinosum.
rationales.b: Lesser petrosal nerve passes via foramen ovale or canaliculus innominatus rather than spinosum.
rationales.c: Maxillary nerve exits middle cranial fossa through foramen rotundum.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q005.takeaway: Mastication muscles receive V3 motor supply, which exits skull through foramen ovale.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q005.displayText: Bruxism or teeth grinding mainly involves the temporalis, lateral pterygoids and masseter muscles of mastication. These are supplied by the mandibular nerve. It passes through the foramen ovale (marked A in the explanation figure). The other foramina marked are foramen spinosum, foramen lacerum and jugular foramen.

rationales.b: Foramen spinosum is the small posterolateral opening for middle meningeal artery, not V3 motor fibers.
rationales.c: Foramen lacerum is largely fibrocartilage-filled and is not the mandibular nerve exit.
rationales.d: Jugular foramen carries CN IX–XI and venous structures, not V3.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q006.displayText: The image shows the sphenoid bone. The foramen marked is the foramen rotundum. The maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve passes through it.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q007.takeaway: Sigmoid sinus occupies posterior jugular foramen; CN IX–XI pass its intermediate compartment.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q007.displayText: Vernet's syndrome or jugular foramen syndrome refers to palsies of the IX, X and XI cranial nerves traversing the jugular foramen. The sigmoid sinus passes through the posterior aspect of the jugular foramen. The jugular foramen can be divided into three compartments: anterior - inferior petrosal sinus; intermediate - CN IX, X and XI; posterior - sigmoid sinus continuing as the internal jugular vein. Arteries passing through include the meningeal branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery and the meningeal branch of the occipital artery; emissary veins may also traverse it.

rationales.a: Spinal accessory nerve passes through the intermediate jugular compartment with IX–XI, not posterior compartment.
rationales.c: Inferior petrosal sinus occupies anterior compartment.
rationales.d: Vagus nerve passes through intermediate compartment, while sigmoid sinus occupies posterior part.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q008.takeaway: Membrana tectoria, continuous with posterior longitudinal ligament, passes through foramen magnum.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q008.displayText: The membrana tectoria of the atlanto-axial joint passes through the foramen magnum. The source diagram shows structures passing through the two compartments of the foramen magnum, including its anterior and neurovascular/posterior compartments.

rationales.a: Transverse ligament of atlas lies posterior to dens and does not pass through foramen magnum as the named membrane.
rationales.c: Anterior longitudinal ligament continues over vertebral bodies and does not form the membrane crossing the craniovertebral aperture.
rationales.d: Ligamentum flavum lies between laminae; membrana tectoria passes superiorly through foramen magnum.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q009.takeaway: Inferior alveolar nerve is anesthetized at mandibular foramen for mandibular teeth.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q009.displayText: The marked structure is the mandibular foramen and the inferior alveolar nerve passes through it. The inferior alveolar nerve is blocked by injecting a local anaesthetic at the mandibular foramen. The source also shows the landmark used for an inferior alveolar nerve block.

rationales.a: Lingual nerve is in floor of mouth and carries general sensation/taste, not the nerve anesthetized at mandibular foramen.
rationales.b: Mandibular nerve is proximal trunk; the local block at foramen targets its inferior alveolar branch.
rationales.c: Chorda tympani joins lingual nerve in infratemporal fossa and does not pass through mandibular foramen.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q010.takeaway: CN III traverses intermediate compartment of superior orbital fissure within common tendinous ring.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q010.displayText: The marked structure is the superior orbital fissure and the oculomotor nerve passes through this foramen. The superior orbital fissure is divided into three compartments by the common tendinous ring. The oculomotor nerve passes through its intermediate compartment.

rationales.b: Olfactory nerve passes through cribriform plate.
rationales.c: Optic nerve passes through optic canal.
rationales.d: Facial nerve exits via internal acoustic meatus and stylomastoid foramen, not superior orbital fissure.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q011.takeaway: Abducens nerve enters orbit via superior orbital fissure within common tendinous ring.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q011.displayText: The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure and the abducens nerve passes through it. The abducens nerve is the 6th cranial nerve and arises from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction. It runs through Dorello's canal at the medial end of the petrous ridge, enters the cavernous sinus where it lies lateral to the internal carotid artery, then enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the common tendinous ring and supplies the lateral rectus. Other options: the spinal accessory nerve passes through the foramen magnum; the ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal with the optic nerve; the middle meningeal artery and vein pass through the foramen spinosum with the meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve.

rationales.b: Spinal accessory nerve enters posterior triangle and exits skull via jugular foramen, not orbital fissure.
rationales.c: Ophthalmic artery enters orbit through optic canal, not superior orbital fissure.
rationales.d: Middle meningeal artery enters skull through foramen spinosum.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q012.takeaway: Maxilla contributes most to orbital floor.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q012.displayText: The X-ray shows a fracture of the floor of the orbit. The maxilla makes the maximum contribution to the floor of the orbit. The source lists the boundaries and constituent bones of the bony orbit: the roof is formed principally by the orbital plate of the frontal bone with the lesser wing of sphenoid posteriorly; the floor includes the orbital plate of maxilla, zygomatic bone and orbital process of palatine bone; the medial wall includes maxilla, lacrimal bone, ethmoid bone and sphenoid; and the lateral wall includes zygomatic bone and greater wing of sphenoid. The orbital floor can fracture after trauma to the orbit, with orbital contents herniating into the maxillary sinus and producing a teardrop-like appearance.

rationales.b: Sphenoid contributes to orbital apex and roof, but maxilla forms most of orbital floor.
rationales.c: Palatine contributes a small posterior part of floor, not the maximal portion.
rationales.d: Zygomatic contributes lateral floor but less than maxilla.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q013.takeaway: Supraorbital nerve exits notch/foramen at point C, the junction of medial and lateral thirds of orbital margin.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q013.displayText: Upper eyelid lacerations are sutured under a supraorbital nerve block. Anaesthesia is achieved by approaching the nerve at the supraorbital foramen/notch. The supraorbital notch is present at the junction of the lateral two-thirds and medial one-third of the supraorbital margin (point C). It transmits the supraorbital nerve and vessels.

rationales.b: Point B lies elsewhere along the orbital margin and is not the supraorbital nerve landmark.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q014.takeaway: Pterion overlies the lesser wing of sphenoid and anterior division of middle meningeal artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q014.displayText: The structure marked in the image is the pterion, and the bony structure present behind it is the lesser wing of the sphenoid. The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull: frontal bone, squamous part of the temporal bone, greater wing of sphenoid bone and parietal bone. The anterior division of the middle meningeal artery lies deep to it. It also overlies the lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere, so a hematoma can cause compressive lesions there.

rationales.a: Clivus is posterior cranial base, not the bone beneath the pterion.
rationales.c: Sella turcica is central sphenoid body and not the lateral pterion landmark.
rationales.d: Carotid canal lies in petrous temporal bone, not deep to pterion.
